1.	What is the present capacity of our existing terrestrial microwave relay telecommunications system?
2.	Does the government have any forecast regarding the capacity utilization of our present terrestrial
January 22, 1969

microwave relay telecommunications system for the next 5, 10, 15, 20 years?
3.	Is the proposed satellite system less expensive or more than the present microwave setup and over what distances?

In so far as communications is concerned:
1.	There are currently two main terrestrial national microwave radio relay telecommunication systems in operation: the Trans-Canada Telephone System; and the CN/CP Telecommunication System.
The capacity varies; however, there is a working minimum of five, two-way broadband radio frequency (TV equivalent) channels in use today throughout the major portion of these coast-to-coast systems, including their many spurs.
The above systems are located south of the 55th parallel. In addition, CN/CP have placed in operation a broadband microwave route from Alberta through Northern British Columbia and the Yukon to Alaska. This system has one two-way working channel (300 circuits) at present.
2.	Forecasts of additional utilization for the microwave systems for several years into the future are very difficult to make because other technological forms of communication may become more attractive and because the total demand for service is difficult to predict. Using present growth rates the total utilization of all systems might double every five years, but it does not necessarily follow that this growth rate would continue in future.
The additional potential capacity of these national microwave systems if and when augmented, coast to coast, could be up to 23 twoway broadband channels, of which 11 would extend for approximately 2/3 of the route length.
Each of these channels would have a capacity in both directions of one television signal or a varying quantity of 600-1200 voice-data circuits per channel. The CN/CP Alberta-Yukon system could be augmented to carry 4 additional channels.
3.	A direct comparison of costs of a satellite system and a terrestrial microwave relay system is very difficult to make because the two systems are not directly comparable. In general, the cost of a terrestrial microwave system is proportional to distance, whereas
Questions
satellite system costs are independent of the distance between earth stations.

ALLEGED PARALYSIS OF WHEAT MOVEMENT THROUGH VANCOUVER-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I ask
leave, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin, in accordance with the terms of revised Standing Order 26, to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the virtual bottleneck and paralysis of wheat movement in Vancouver Harbour, due to the failure of the government to work with the railways in scheduling box cars, leading to a situation which has already resulted in the loss of a 17,000 ton contract and which may result in the loss of others; which has caused damage and economic loss, since some ships have been tied up for as long as a month, paying demurrage charges as high as $2,500 a day; which has brought about stagnation in the movement of wheat at a critical time for western farmers; and in connection with which the government, yesterday, in the person of the minister, refused to take action.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: ALLEGED PARALYSIS OF WHEAT MOVEMENT THROUGH VANCOUVER-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member for Mackenzie has given notice as required by Standing Order 26 of his intention to move the adjournment of the house to discuss the matter raised in his proposed motion.
An hon. members know, the provisions of Standing Order 26 have been radically altered in the new rules of procedure of the House of Commons. Under the terms of paragraph (5) of Standing Order 26, in determining whether a matter should be given urgent consideration, the Chair takes into account the extent to which the proposition concerns the administrative responsibilities of the government or would come within the scope of ministerial action, and also the probability of the matter being brought before the house within a reasonable time by other means. Additionally, the Chair must have regard to other considerations, many of which have been established as the practice of the house in previous years, before the enactment of the present Standing Orders.
The question raised by the hon. member, it seems to me, does concern the administrative responsibilities of the government.
As far as the opportunity for the question being raised before the house within a reasonable time by other means is concerned, the Chair must have in mind the fact that in the present state of its business the house is not likely to have available certain opportunities which on previous occasions would have provided a vehicle for a debate on this question. As an example, there is no current debate in respect to the Speech from the Throne. We learned from the Minister of Finance yesterday that there is some uncertainty whether or not there will be a budget debate within the near future, and the estimates are not likely to be tabled until some time in February.
There is another matter which I think may be of some importance, and that has to do with the alteration in circumstances surrounding emergency debates before the enactment of the current Standing Order 26. Before the present order was brought into force, in considering motions to adjourn under Standing Order 26 the Chair always had to weigh the importance of the proposed motion against the necessity of setting aside government business for the day and it was much more difficult to justify the granting of a motion under Standing Order 26 when that would have the result of delaying current important public business. To a considerable extent the revised Standing Order 26 reduces the relative significance of this factor.
January 22, 1969

In deciding whether or not to allow the motion the Chair must, of course, take into account the actual problem sought to be discussed. Is it of national importance and is it urgent?
In my opinion the new circumstances indicated by the questions asked in the house yesterday, by the concern expressed by the minister himself when replying to these questions, and by the hon. member's statement, indicate that a strong case can be made in favour of the proposed motion, on the ground of urgency of debate.
Therefore I am inclined to put the question to the house in accordance with the standing order for the reasons stated, that the matter is important, that there is urgency of debate, that the opportunity for debate within a reasonable time is restricted, and that public business is not impeded.
The question before the house is the following one. Has the hon. member leave to move the motion for the purpose of discussing the matter stated by him?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT SUBSTITUTING RATE PRESCRIBED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the passage of Bill C-151 but I would like to take this opportunity to say a few words about it. This bill is an act to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, and yesterday I listened with interest to some of the debate on the bill.
I am not going to try to cover the ground which several hon. members from the Atlantic provinces covered in connection with the use to which this bill could and should be put. However, I do protest to the minister and the government against the clause in the bill which removes the 5 per cent ceiling on interest rates and leaves it up to the Governor in Council to set the interest rate which fishermen must pay for loans under this act. It seems to me that the government, in this field as in others, is moving in the wrong direction.
A number of hon. members referred to a lack of use by fishermen generally of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. I am quite certain that the increase in interest rates, which is bound to come about by the removal of the 5 per cent maximum rate, is going to do nothing to encourage fishermen to take out loans under this act.
I was very pleased to see the minister and other hon. members make reference to the excellent record of fishermen in regard to the repayment of loans under the act. I agree with other members that this should be broadcast widely. It is very interesting to note that in 13 years only nine loans, amounting to a small total of just over $3,000, have not been repaid. I do not think any other group in Canada can match this record, and the fishermen and their organizations can be very proud of the people in their ranks.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
In going over the information given to the house yesterday it seems apparent to me that in some parts of Canada fishermen or fishermen's unions are not taking advantage of the loans available under this bill. I should like to pose a question or two to the minister. Has he or his department checked to see why the fishermen and their organizations have not made greater use of this act as a means of obtaining improvement loans? It seems to me it would be logical for fishermen to make the best possible use of this legislation when they needed loans for the improvement of their
January 22, 1969

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act fishing equipment. I was amazed to learn of the small number of loans which had been taken out over the years. I would appreciate it very much if the minister when he winds up the debate could tell us why the fishermen in certain provinces in particular appeared extremely reluctant to seek assistance under this measure.
Finally, I repeat my complaint about the raising of the present maximum interest rate of 5 per cent. Throughout this session we find the government doing the same thing in connection with all new loan legislation. In my opinion this is not the way to bring relief to people who apply for assistance and desperately need it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposed amendments to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act are certainly in the interests of the fisheries industry in all parts of Canada. During this debate some hon. members have attempted to suggest there were provincial motives involved on the part of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis). I do not think inferences of this kind have any place whatever in the House of Commons.
An unfair inference was drawn yesterday by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) that because the minister comes from British Columbia he had in some way worked against the great province of Newfoundland and other provinces in this country. Such an allegation is unworthy of this assembly. An attempt was made to divert the attention of the house from the real merits of the bill before us. It is a good bill, a bill which will provide a great deal of credit to help fishermen to build new boats, to equip their boats better, and to become more effective wherever they may fish.
The number of lending institutions is being increased. The interest rate is being made more flexible and more realistic. If the hon. member for St. John's East had any knowledge whatsoever of economics he would surely welcome this change. Loans may be made for a wider range of purposes than ever before. The minister, who needs no one to defend him because he is doing a good job in the office he holds, invited suggestions from the opposition with regard to a new limit on the total amount of loans to fishermen. Instead of constructive proposals we heard a diatribe unsupported by the facts. The minister pointed out that in 1955 the limit was $4,000 and that in 1965 there was a limit of $10,000. He suggested that perhaps $25,000 
would be a realistic new limit and asked the opposition to make constructive proposals for changes in this area. What did we get? A total absence of constructive thought.

Again we hear divisive talk from the hon. member. It is fortunate we have Hansard because in an earlier year the hon. member, who was then assistant to one of the ministers, made a speech in the house. That was on May 12, 1961. The ground rules were different then, however, when this outspoken Conservative critic was a backbencher supporting a Conservative government. This is what he had to say then; I quote from page 4735 of Hansard:
I realize that all too often people speaking on this subject tend to generalize and to oversimplify, and I hppe that this afternoon I will not be too guilty of generalization, bearing in mind at all times that I do not have a really technical knowledge of this very complex subject.
He was uttering truth, Mr. Speaker. This is indeed a complex question. No one in Canada can remain unconcerned about this problem whether he lives in British Columbia or on the prairies or in the maritimes, because we are a united country.
I trust the hon. member is as concerned about the problems we face in British Columbia as we in British Columbia are concerned about the future of the maritimes. At an earlier period in his political career it seems the hon. member had a more highly developed spirit of candour. He said:
I think you have here the real weakness of the Canadian salt fish industry, the fact that our markets for this product depend upon the stocks or supplies of the European markets. It is a common fact that most of the European markets are supplied generally by their own subsidized fleets operating in most cases in Canadian waters.
Of course it is a fact. It continues to be a fact today. But the same hon. member who told us in 1961 that the problem did not lend itself to oversimplification now asks the Minister of Fisheries to stand up and provide instant solutions to the difficulties of the Newfoundland fishermen. He knew in 1961 when he was defending his own government that this was impossible, that this was one of the problem areas.
The other day the hon. member for St. John's East accused other members of this house of knowing nothing about Newfoundland. "You haven't even been there", he said. Mr. Speaker, I have always wanted to go to

Mr. Speaker, I hope that the point has been made as to the divergence between the statements made when the hon. member was defending his government in facing this problem and the statements that he made yesterday. In his speech we were told that there is a lack of assistance to the province of Newfoundland from the federal government. If the hon. member would become active in supporting this legislation, which is going to increase the amount of money that can be borrowed by those engaged in the fishing industry and make it available at realistic interest rates, he would be making a more constructive contribution on the part of his province than the contribution he made yesterday.
Under the provincial program, 10 per cent of the cost of a boat is available through a provincial subsidy at an interest rate of 3.5 per cent, repayable in ten years. On used equipment there is a 25 per cent subsidy, also at 3.5 per cent interest and repayable in ten years. That was one reason there were only 18 fisheries improvement loans in Newfoundland over the period cited by the hon. member in his speech.
How is this provincial assistance made available? It is because federal government development dollars amount to more than 30 cents for every $1 spent for all purposes in Newfoundland. Yet the hon. member from Newfoundland has told us that the government is doing nothing for Newfoundland and for Newfoundland fishermen, that the minister is, in effect, a liar. He would do better to support this measure, get behind it, and do a

personal public relations job in Newfoundland by encouraging those in the fishing industry in the province to examine the legislation very carefully so as to find out whether or not they may qualify, and thus render a real service to his province. I understand that, Mr. Speaker. It is unfortunate that the hon. member's remarks misrepresented the facts of a situation. No one will deny that in presenting Bill C-151 the Minister of Fisheries is trying to make an effort, in one form or another, to help the fishermen of Canada ameliorate their
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act circumstances. One of our problems is that the Minister of Fisheries does not know the Atlantic region. His sincerity notwithstanding, he has not had a great deal to do with the Atlantic fishery. It might be a good idea if we had two deputy ministers responsible for fisheries, one dealing with the Atlantic region and one with the Pacific coast. Because there are great differences between the east and west coast fisheries I have heard it suggested that there ought to be two ministers responsible for fisheries who in turn would have deputy ministers. Although no one can say that the minister is displaying no interest in our fisheries it is true that he knows little about Atlantic Canada. I think he will be the first to admit that.
It is well for the minister to understand that our Atlantic fishermen are not looking for handouts or for government of Canada doles. I take strong exception to any suggestion that under Bill C-151 our fishermen will be entitled to receive a form of dole. That kind of thinking is unworthy of some of our better off Canadians who live in industrialized regions. It is unjust for anyone to classify some people in Canada as second class citizens who are satisfied to live on government handouts. Anyone making that suggestion about our Atlantic fishermen is wasting the time of hon. members and of this house.
Several times during this debate hon. members have mentioned that the fishermen of Newfoundland receive 40 per cent of their total incomes in the form of government handouts. Only last month the government of Canada made a so-called sacrifice and shipped 50 million pounds of fish to Biafra. The world looked on and said, "My, what a government they have in Canada; what a great government." The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) was happy with the shipment, everyone was happy, and representatives at the United Nations acclaimed the magnificently benevolent attitude Canada displayed toward the suffering people of Nigeria and Biafra. We sent the fish all right, but what the people of the world did not understand was that the government of Canada squeezed the fishermen of Newfoundland in order to obtain that fish at the lowest possible price. It was the fishermen of Newfoundland who made the sacrifice and who shipped that fish to Biafra.

As a result some fishermen in Newfoundland were paid as little as $13 per hundredweight of fish, the price last year having been $27 a hundredweight. Yesterday evening the minister outlined the aims of this legislation, as found on page 4581 of Hansard. No one will question the ultimate aims of Bill C-151. We all want to see the fishermen of Atlantic Canada and other parts of the country benefit from the legislation. Yet the fact remains that few have made use of this legislation in the past. Merely passing this bill is like saying to our fishermen: There are fish in the water. The fact remains that the oceans are large. The question is, where are the fish? In the past fishermen did not know of the provisions of similar legislation. They did not know they could obtain money. Not many loans were made under this legislation last year, and the hon. member for Bur-naby-Seymour and the Minister of Fisheries are aware of that fact. Will it be the responsibility of the Minister of Fisheries, the Minister of Finance or anyone else charged with the administration of this legislation to make known to our fishermen the provisions of this legislation? The government allocated $500 to make known to the fishermen of Newfoundland the provisions of previous legislation. That was not enough. Our fishermen must be made aware of the provisions of this legislation.
The fact is that since our fishermen live in little coves and inlets they cannot receive messages through the mass communications media as readily as the citizens of Toronto or other metropolitan centres. Our fishermen should know of the benefits they can derive from Bill C-151, how they can apply for loans, pay those loans back, and what they must do if they get into difficulties and cannot make payments for a number of years. The government may have to hire public relations people to make known the benefits of this legislation, or it could be done through inspectors. It is a waste of time enacting laws to benefit our fishermen if they do not know of those laws.

automatically bring the ceiling down to 5 per cent or less. If the government of Canada some day in the future can borrow money at 3 per cent, then loans to fishermen will be available at no more than 4 per cent. If the government can borrow at 4 per cent over any period of months, then the fishermen will be able to obtain money for less than 5 per cent, and so on.
This interest rate is part of the general rate structure. As interest rates rise this rate will rise and as interest rates fall it will fall. It will always be a preferred rate relative to the rate large corporations would pay and certainly will be preferential over the rate at which small companies might borrow from the Industrial Development Bank and the rate which most small commercial establishments would have to pay on loans made through a bank or other commercial lending institution. This is good legislation in the sense that it gives preference to the fisherman. It gives a preference to him in the sense that he will pay less for money than he would otherwise have to pay.
There are only a few other points on which I should like to touch. There is the question of the maximum loan which can be granted. This was raised by the hon. member for Bur-naby-Richmond (Mr. Goode). This was the reason I asked one of the members what the amount would be that a fisherman would need to finance a new vessel. I would like to know what it would cost a fisherman today to finance a new longliner on the east coast, for example, or a new halibut boat on the west coast. Would the amount be $10,000 or would it more likely be $30,000, $40,000 or $50,000? If this is the amount of money a fisherman must have in order to equip himself with a new vessel including all the necessary electronic gear and so on, then we should consider a ceiling higher than the ceiling of $10,000 which has been in effect since 1965. This, however, is a matter on which we can obtain expert opinion and evidence when the bill is before the committee.
Several members have asked why these loans are not used more. In the Atlantic region, generally speaking there is provincial legislation under which loans are available at lower interest rates than are available now from private lenders. Also in some provinces there are direct grants available as well; in other words, interest-free money which in many cases is given and forgotten by the province. The lender in all these cases is the provincial government. One can perhaps

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act make a case for direct loans by the federal government but we are not discussing direct loans today. We are discussing loans made available by private lenders with a federal government guarantee. This is parallel legislation to the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
I do not think there are any other points on which I should dwell now because we should get this legislation before the committee where I am sure all interested members will do their very best to improve it from the fisherman's point of view.

the second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs of Bill C-152, to amend the Veterans Land Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it may not be necessary to speak at any length on this bill as hon. members are familiar in general terms with the Veterans Land Act. Perhaps I should mention that since the act became effective in 1942, some 117,000 veterans have taken advantage of its financial assistance to establish themselves on farms or small holdings. The total investment of funds for that purpose has amounted to $911 million. At the present time the department has approximately 56,000 active accounts representing an investment of $438 million. These figures clearly demonstrate that the V.L.A. has been a major factor in the re-establishment of Canadian veterans.
Veterans Land Act
The purpose of the proposed amendment in this bill is to provide that certain interest rates charged on moneys lent under the Veterans Land Act may be prescribed by the Governor in Council instead of being fixed by statute. Hon. members are well aware that interest rates in the general economy of the country fluctuate from time to time and have in recent years been somewhat above the long term level.
At the present time the V.L.A. has three different rates, two of them fixed by statute and the third prescribed by regulation. The rate of interest on loans up to $6,000 was established in 1942 at 3J per cent which was close to the cost of money at that time. For loans over $6,000 and under $20,000 the rate of 5 per cent was fixed by statute in 1954. For farm loans in excess of $20,000 the rate is determined by the Governor in Council and since 1964 has been related directly to that charged under the Farm Credit Act. This third rate is currently 7J per cent.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The effect of the proposed measure would be to transfer the rate for loans over $6,000 and under $20,000, which is now 5 per cent, from a statutory to a regulatory basis. It will permit the rate to be established from time to time by the Governor in Council. Hon. members will recall that the house recently considered a measure to amend the Farm Credit Act so that the interest rate under that plan might similarly be prescribed by regulation. The principle in both cases is the same. Following enactment of this measure it is the intention to apply the same interest rates for V.L.A. loans over $6,000 as those that are applied from time to time for the whole amount of loans under the Farm Credit Act.
I should like to emphasize that this measure will not affect the 31 per cent rate on the repayable portion of V.L.A. loans up to $6,000 under part I of the act. This rate has been unchanged since 1942 and will remain on a statutory basis as at present. The conditional grant paid for ten years continued occupancy of the house by the veteran will also remain unchanged. The government recognizes the special position of veterans and regards the benefits outlined in the Veterans Charter as an entitlement for war service in War II or the Korean forces. Part I of the Veterans Land Act is one of these benefits included in the Veterans Charter. Therefore, although the 3i per cent rate is now substantially below the cost of long term money, veterans who

January 22, 1969
Veterans Land Act
are established in the future will continue to receive this benefit.
Under the new arrangement the veteran borrower will pay 3| per cent on the part I portion of the loan and a rate fixed by order in council on the remainder. It will be seen that the average of the two rates will vary with the total size of the loan. For example, under the provisions of the bill a newly established smallholder who obtains approval of an $18,000 loan with interest at 3J per cent and 7f per cent would pay an average rate of 6J per cent on the repayable debt of $14,000. Similarly, a veteran being established as a farmer and obtaining the maximum loan of $40,000 with a repayable debt of $37,200 for a period of 30 years would in the present circumstances be charged an average rate calculated at 7.4 per cent.
I might mention that the new rates will not affect applications received before September 13, 1968, and applications received after that date and approved before the coming into force of this bill will also fall under the old rates. Existing contracts remain unaffected. If, however, additional loans are approved after the bill becomes law, the new rate will apply but only to the amount of the new loans.
The preservation of the statutory 3J per cent rate on part I loans produces an average rate which is materially lower than the interest rates paid for other kinds of mortgage loans. This in my view should be acceptable to the veterans of Canada because it maintains their preferred position in obtaining financial assistance under the act. I therefore trust that Bill C-152 will be referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs for detailed study.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of parliament and the Canadian people have been taken in very badly by the Liberal government in the last
Veterans Land Act
two or three years, particularly the low income groups. A few years ago we listened to the then minister of finance indicate that if the ceiling on the bank interest rate were raised-I can well remember the argument- interest rates would probably level out at about 4 per cent, that we would destroy the secondary lending institutions such as trust companies, finance companies and other institutions, and that the prime interest rate would come down considerably below the 6 per cent ceiling. It is an indication of how little most of us know about finance and about the methods used in financing that we did not even realize we were being hoodwinked at that time. Since then we have been continually faced with increasing rates on loans under specific legislation.
I was very concerned when the interest rate on farm credit under the Farm Credit Corporation was raised because these were long term loans that were being subsidized by the government to enable farmers across Canada to upgrade their farm operations and make them more economic. The same was true of farm improvement loans. Farm syndicates were in a different category because there was no fixed interest rate on such loans and there was some merit in freeing it. The fisheries legislation we have just discussed is in the same category. Loans were subsidized to assist in upgrading the operations of fishermen, particularly on the east coast.
Now we are faced with changes in the Veterans Land Act. In my opinion it is a good thing that the Canadian people in 1945 decided, in establishing the Veterans Land Act, to use this method rather than the old soldier settlement scheme which was so badly abused by governments, and to create this charter in such a way as to permit veterans to establish themselves on farms with special advantages.
I sincerely congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs for having been able to retain part I where the interest rate stands at 3i per cent for loans up to $6,000. I think this is a reward to those who gave up, if nothing else, several years of their lives in the service of their country. It seems there are not many people in the government who have sympathy for the veterans and their problems. Therefore I assume the Minister of Veterans Affairs should be congratulated for having been able to retain part I, especially in view of the fact that the government seems hell-bent on balancing the budget at the expense of the little people. High interest rates will certainly not be a help in this regard. We know that

January 22, 1969
Veterans Land Act
when the government borrows money at 6i per cent and then lends it to the veterans at 5 per cent there is a cost to the taxpayer, but we have some responsibility to the veterans. We established the 5 per cent interest rate when capital was being borrowed at under 3 per cent, and it seems to me that this will balance off so that the government will not lose much in this operation.
The Veterans Land Act has been operated very successfully, both by the present director and the previous one who sincerely believe in the principle of self-help for the veterans. The whole program has been a great success. It seems to me a great shame that we have not been able to maintain over a period of 30 years the same type of legislation for one veteran as against another. The cost of loans under part II and part III will probably run to 7| per cent.
Very recently we increased the interest rate on national housing loans which we now find are running as high as 9.58 per cent. It seems to me quite possible that before long loans under the Veterans Land Act, the Farm Credit Corporation, and our other fixed, long term, assured loans, will carry interest rates of 8 or 9 per cent as well.
The hon. member who just spoke suggested we should not discuss this bill at length on second reading but refer it to the committee. I am of the same opinion because it presents us with a fait accompli and there is absolutely nothing we can do about it. The government will need $500 million to meet its commitments and it will have to borrow. It will lend at an interest rate 1 per cent above its borrowing rate, which will mean a rate of 7-2 to 8 per cent. In my opinion there is nothing the committee can do about it; the committee can only muck around long enough to weaken the position of the minister in retaining the rate of 3J per cent on the first $6,000. It seems to me there is nothing to be gained by sending this legislation to the committee or, indeed, by sending any legislation involving higher interest rates to committees. I think the country has been hoodwinked into believing we have really done something in the seven or eight bills we have recently dealt with, but we really have no influence whatever on their content in relation to interest rates. The rate is actually being set by the Minister of

Finance (Mr. Benson) who determines the government's over-all policy, which is to produce a balanced budget regardless of where the revenue comes from.
As it happens, the funds necessary for these loans are not available from any other source. Take veterans established under the Veterans Land Act, for example. For many reasons, the only borrowing sources open to them are these government institutions. Parliament, in my view, has no say in regard to the changes which are taking place and there is nothing in this bill which warrants sending it to the committee. I would be prepared, and I think members of my party would be prepared, to waive consideration by the committee. The interest rate is a fait accompli and there is nothing else to be discussed. We took part in a discussion concerning the Veterans Land Act a year ago when we were told there was a cut-off of applications for benefit under the Veterans Charter. We know how many applications there are, we know the need which exists, at least approximately, and there does not seem to be much that we can change in this connection.
I think we should let the country know that the government is failing to honour its commitments. Some of those commitments were made, it is true, by people who have gone from this chamber. But the commitments with respect to the Veterans Charter were entered upon not by one party alone but by every political party in a non-partisan manner. The commitment was by the House of Commons, by the government as a continuing entity, and it should remain in effect as long as there is a need for the benefits of the charter.
It is a breach of faith, in my opinion, when the interest rate is changed-a rate which was obviously subsidized as a result of decisions by people who knew what they were doing and wanted to give some return to the veterans of Canada for the services they had rendered. We have reached a sad pass when we have to ask veterans to pick up part of the tab because we in Canada have not been able to keep our financial institutions in line with the needs of our people.

Mr. Speaker, to speak briefly this afternoon on Bill C-152, may I begin by drawing attention to the fact that when ministers speak in closing debates on bills with a similar provision they invariably suggest that the funds required by the people who need to borrow cannot be made available as formerly because

the terms are no longer acceptable to the major financial institutions. This bill is another indication that the money people are telling the government of the day exactly what to do and where to get off. I agree that the minister is to be congratulated on retaining a rate of 3J per cent on that portion of each loan up to $6,000. I feel that in the other bills which have come before us consideration should have been given to a provision of the same kind, but there is nothing we can do about that now. Only time and elections will provide the answer.
There is just one point I should like to dwell on. How have we allowed ourselves to become so deeply involved with the banks and the finance companies? Every time we turn around we find the banks and finance companies telling us what to do. And up to now there has not been a government big enough to put these institutions in their place. In my opinion this country is run entirely by these financial institutions and it is high time we in parliament had a say, through the government, in setting interest rates.
How is it that these finance companies, and the banks especially, always show such huge profits? We have read the latest financial statements of some of the banks and we have seen that while interest rates are rising their profits are constantly increasing. No one argues that individuals who invest their money are not entitled to a fair return, but I submit that a fair return on investment means a rate of interest which the people of Canada can at least afford to pay. It is time the government did something about this and used a stick on these institutions.
Another question bothers me when I consider Bill C-152 and similar measures in which interest rates play such an important part. What are the financial institutions really contributing to the welfare of our society in general? Somehow they get money out of the people, lend it back to them at high interest rates, and up go their profits. It seems to me these institutions provide nothing tangible for the benefit of the society in which we live. We know that the farmers, the fishermen, the labourers of this country, produce food and contribute to the general well-being. I suggest that until real thought is given to our monetary system the people of Canada will have nothing to be proud of as far as our financial institutions are concerned. written has been produced by a pulp mill which employs workmen to manufacture the finished product. There is no reasoning behind the system under which we are living.

So I think they have given quite a lot. As a matter of fact, we should be proud of our banking system in Canada. None of them has gone broke, as happened in the United States not so many years ago. I suggest our banking system has led Canada forward a long way and that we should be proud of it.
To get back to the bill now before the house, I and I am sure many other government backbenchers are sick and tired of the sermons that are periodically delivered to us by members of the opposition in connection with the high cost of money. He said: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
You
had better be good.

-I wish to present to the house for consideration Bill S-14, which deals with amendments to the Aeronautics Act. As hon. members know, this act regulates and controls civil aviation in Canada. Part I of the act is administered by the Minister of Transport and deals generally with the licensing and operation of air crews, aircraft and airports. Part II comes under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Transport Commission and deals with the licensing and operation of commercial air services. Part III applies generally to employees who are charged with the administration of the act and also deals with prosecutions for violations of the act and regulations.

January 22, 1969
Aeronautics Act
I should like to describe briefly the main amendments which are proposed under this bill. Clause 2 of the bill would enable the Governor in Council to authorize the Minister of Transport, subject to conditions and in lieu of the Governor in Council, to prescribe changes for the use of facilities and services which are provided by the Department of Transport in respect of aircraft or departmental airports. For example, automobile parking fees at airports must now be established by an order in council. The amendment, however, would enable the Governor in Council to authorize the Minister of Transport to prescribe such fees.
Clause 3 of the bill would authorize the Minister of Transport to delegate to the Deputy Minister of Transport the former's authority to make orders prohibiting or restricting the navigation of aircraft over specified areas during certain periods of time. This is to accommodate military air exercises. To expedite the obtaining of the necessary prohibition orders the Minister of Transport would authorize his deputy minister to make these orders.
Clause 4(1) and clause 9 amend the definition of aircraft in order to exclude hovercraft from the Aeronautics Act, as hovercraft are being brought under the Canada Shipping Act by an amendment to that act which is now before parliament. Because of the manner in which hovercraft operate they cannot be controlled and administered efficiently under the Aeronautics Act. Although hovercraft employ a form of flight one can hardly describe a vehicle that hovers between 6 and 18 inches from the ground as flying. Hovercraft as well as air-cushioned vehicles constitute a special method of transportation and are dissimilar to aeroplanes in almost every respect. They operate in an environment that conventional aircraft do not operate in.
Clause 4(2) of the bill amends section 6 of the act in order to authorize the Canadian Transport Commission to issue temporary licences for commercial air services, an example being seasonal licences or emergency licences.
Clauses 5 and 6 of the bill amend certain sections of the act in order to make it clear that the powers of the commission are confined to part II of the act only. Clause 7 amends section 13, to clarify the power of the Canadian Transport Commission to make regulations of general application with respect to commercial air services. Prior approval of such regulations would not be required by the Governor in Council. However, it

should be pointed out that subsection 2 of section 13 would give to the Governor in Council the power contained in section 53 of the Railway Act to vary and rescind such regulations.
Clause 8 of the bill includes provisions respecting proof of documents in order to provide that copies of documents purporting to be certified by the secretary of the Department of Transport shall be true copies of the original documents on record or issued by the Department of Transport and also that such documents shall be prima facie evidence in prosecutions under part I. This clause further provides that a certificate from the secretary of the Department of Transport stating that no licence or certificate has been issued by the department will also be prima facie evidence in such prosecutions.
Although the proposed amendments to the Aeronautics Act I have just outlined are necessary and desirable improvements to the act, none of the amendments alters the underlying basis of the act. I therefore recommend Bill S-14, to amend the Aeronautics Act, for the consideration of the house, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I arrived in the house too late to hear the minister's introductory remarks. It seems to me that in this bill the government is endeavouring to cure an omission in legislation which recently was the subject matter of litigation before the Supreme Court. I take it that is why clause 7 of the bill has been included. It seeks to cure that deficiency. I do not know whether the minister dealt with that deficiency in his introductory remarks. If he did not I hope he will do so in his remarks closing the debate.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I believe the bill in itself is indicative of a very unfortunate trend to enlarge the areas of rule by regulation. It provides almost unlimited powers, in this case not for the Governor in Council but for an administrative tribunal, to make regulations which are not even required to be submitted for approval to the cabinet. This is a very undesirable trend. I am speaking now of clause 2 of the bill, but more particularly I am speaking of the power which the bill, if adopted, will provide to the Air Transport Commission to make regulations without any requirement to submit them to the minister or to the cabinet for approval. It is an extremely undesirable state of affairs.
Here we have an industry, general aviation-I am not now speaking of the huge
January 22, 1969

international and national carriers such as Air Canada, and Canadian Pacific Airlines but of the industry in terms of the charter operators, both regional and smaller-which is going to be required to submit to regulations which may be made at the whim of the A.T.C. or a member thereof from time to time. It seems to me that this is a pretty untenable business proposition, quite apart from the suffocating atmosphere it imposes on the industry generally. It is completely wrong for a charter operator to be granted a licence under certain conditions which are imposed upon the licence at the time of its issue and then three or four months or perhaps a year or two later have the Air Transport Commission decide in its own wisdom that the conditions imposed upon the licence at the time of its issue are to be further limited. In this position a charter operator simply does not know where he stands from time to time.
One could go into specifics with respect to different classifications of licences that are granted but I do not think it would be helpful in a forum such as this. Suffice it to pick one example. Let us assume that a charter operator is given a Class A licence out of one of the major cities to operate a non-scheduled charter operation from that city. The restriction imposed upon the licence at the time of its issue might be that the operator will be restricted to the operation of one particular category of aircraft. Let us assume that at a later stage, a year hence, technological improvements result in equipment being available that is faster, safer and more comfortable than the type of equipment covered in the issuance of the licence in the first instance. If it wished the commission could turn a blind eye to such technological improvement and say to the operator: The existing limitation stands and this is all you are going to be permitted to operate. If the equipment happens to be a DC-3 at the time of issuance of the licence and jet improvements come along, so be it, because they may interfere with some other charter operator who may be in more favour with the commission.
I do not suggest for a moment that the commission has favourites, but nevertheless that kind of attitude could be adopted. What happens here is that the Air Transport Commission imposes its judgment on the operations of the carrier in place of what the carrier deems in its best judgment to be best for its business.
Aeronautics Act
I know the reason for the legislation and that the desire of the Air Transport Commission is to see that the public interest is served at all times, but I suggest it is not going to be served by the commission having the power, as proposed in clause 7 of the bill, to change, bend and warp regulations as it pleases. It is an unlimited and most undesirable administrative power placed in the hands of wellmeaning servants of the government on the Air Transport Commission, but nonetheless in the hands of people who in effect are making decisions for business that may not be in the best interests of business itself, decisions that may run entirely contrary to those which are taken by business. If the public interest is being served by an operator in terms of safety, comfort, speed and technological advancement, the decisions of those who made the investment which is providing that service should be the government criteria and not those of some administrative tribunal.
I believe the other amendments proposed in the bill are inconsequential, apart from their undesirability in terms of extending the regulatory powers of government and government boards. But the central and important part of this bill is the amendment about which I have spoken and which would cure a deficiency that became the subject of litigation before the Supreme Court. I believe that in attempting the cure the government may well find itself in a very difficult position in trying to control a creature which it has set up. I do not want to exaggerate because I know that the members of the Air Transport Commission at all times devote themselves to attempting to make their decisions in the public interest, but what is even more fearful about this amendment is the all-embracing, encompassing powers that are given to the commission with respect to the control and day-to-day operation and administration of the general aviation industry.
I hope the minister will deal with that aspect of the matter, and I hope that on second thought he will propose an amendment to clause 7 to pare down these rather extensive and, I submit, undesirable sowers which the government proposes to give to the A.T.C.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that we are on second reading of this bill, which does not allow for questions and answers, but the minister who is piloting the bill will have the right to speak in closing the debate, so perhaps I might use my right to speak for a

minute or two to put a couple of questions to him in the hope that he will speak at the conclusion of the debate and answer them if he can.

Is this the act under which there is supervision over this matter and is the appropriate authority studying this matter in the light of modern conditions and in the light of the strains under which pilots work in modern aircraft?
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I recall an incident some years ago in respect of which some of us felt that the crash, even though in that particular instance there was no loss of life, was due to the fatigue of a pilot who had been on duty for an excessive period of time. It is on the basis of that incident that I put this question to the minister and I hope he will answer it if he can.
The other question I should like to put to him would seem to be related to clause 3 of the bill. I suspect this is the type of clause about which the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has been complaining in that it seems to put authority in the hands of a deputy minister rather than in the hands of a minister, board or commission. Nevertheless, it is being done. I note that it relates to the issuing of orders or directions prohibiting or restricting navigation of aircraft over specified areas. I would like to raise a general question, but I think the easiest way for me to do it, since in this instance one Winnipeg member is talking to another, is to say to the minister there are times when I have had complaints of more noise than seems reasonable from aircraft flying over Winnipeg.
It so happens, since the member for Winnipeg North Centre is speaking to the member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) about this the situation, that it is our two areas from which these complaints seem to come. It seems that the flight paths from the international airport at Winnipeg which go north and west do not bother very many people, but when an aircraft takes off from the airport and goes east right over Weston and the
(Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).]
heart of Winnipeg North Centre the noise is a little hard to take. Also, when an aircraft takes off in a southerly direction over River Heights the people of Winnipeg South complain.
I should like to ask whether under these provisions an effort will be made to cope more effectively with this problem. I do not intend to stand here opposing progress and saying that we should not have modern aircraft because they are noisy, but things do have to be balanced and we must be concerned not only about the right of people to have transportation by air but also about the right of people on the ground not to be unduly disturbed. The question is general but this is what I have in mind.
If we were going into the committee of the whole stage I would have waited to put this question to the minister, but perhaps I can do it in this way. When he replies I hope the minister will answer my two questions.

Mr. Speaker, Bill No. S-14 entitled an act to amend the Aeronautics Act is designed to normalize certain administrative procedures since the Air Transport Board has been replaced by the Canadian Transport Commission.
The act now stipulates that the charges for the use of any facility or service are set by order in council. To my mind, that procedure is slow and the new bill grants the minister the authority to propose indicated changes according to the circumstances.
One of the clauses which, in my opinion, concerns a large part of our population, is clause 3 which authorizes the minister to delegate his powers, under certain circumstances, and to prohibit or limit air navigation over certain specific areas.
Should an area be threatened, and should it become necessary to suddenly prohibit civil air traffic in that area, the minister should, of necessity, have the authority to do so.
I also feel that the additional powers granted the minister, under such circumstances, would be absolutely normal, because the minister represents the government and, due to that, has absolute authority in a matter as important as aeronautics.
In an era when the number of air passengers increases very rapidly, it is imperative that our laws be revised regularly with a view to facilitating their application, and to ensuring maximum security to the users of
January 22, 1969

air services as well as to the crew of the aircraft.
Canadian laws concerning air transport are explicit, very strict, and a matter of special concern to the Canadian government. In spite of that, we have to deplore, from time to time, air crashes like the one which happened on February 7, 1968, at Vancouver.
The inquiry conducted by the Department of Transport at that time clearly showed that all the information requested before landing had been given to the crew. In this particular case, there seems to be evidence of some disagreement between the captain and the first lieutenant and of a conflict about the management of the craft.
The present bill is even more specific about a number of aspects of the Aeronautics Act. These changes have become necessary, because of the fast growth in recent years, of the air transport industry.
Other aspects will have to be reviewed in the future. There should be more concern about the number of hours the air crew have to work at a stretch and this should be subject to an inquiry by the Transport Commission. There is no blame involved here against the personnel or the Commission, but we should not underestimate the importance of ensuring the safety of both the crew and the passengers.
I am a layman in aeronautics, and so are other hon. members, and we should take the advice of experts on the question.
However, I think that the proposed amendments designed to provide the Minister of Transport with increased powers, can be accepted.
The legislation on aeronautics is not meant to inconvenience air carriers and their staff. On the contrary, it is meant to ensure the absolute comfort of passengers and crews.
The government has clearly shown its interest in the future of air transport each year by earmarking important amounts to improve or supplement present air transport facilities.
On the other hand, I am of the opinion that it is imperative for air carriers to provide the Transport Commission and the minister with all the co-operation that is expected from them so as to give the travelling public perfect service and the security they are entitled to demand.

He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill S-19 which I should now like to present to the house for consideration has relation to amendments to the Navigable Waters Protection Act. I am certain that all hon. members recognize the importance of navigation and shipping as one aspect of our over-all transportation system. As its name implies, the Navigable Waters Protection Act was originally passed to protect Canada's navigable waters from manmade obstructions.
This act was first passed in 1882. Since that time it has been amended on a number of occasions, most recently in 1956. Changing circumstances and particularly the increase in the size of ships require that a number of improvements be made to the act. While I am speaking about the act as a whole in a general way, it might be worth while to point out that the largest number of applications for approval under the act relates to new bridges and repairs to old bridges, as well as to natural gas and fuel pipe lines, transmission lines and telephone lines. Usually these pipe lines or transmission lines are below the surface of navigable waters, but this act also relates to overhead lines which might block navigation. The other man-made works which are of concern are large dams, causeways, log booms and, of course, wharf and docking facilities of all kinds. In fact, anything that is built in the water that could interfere with navigation requires approval under this act.
The act when amended will be in three parts. Part one is concerned primarily with structures that have been designed for specific purposes. Part two is primairly concerned with obstruction to navigation which results accidentally or inadvertently as a consequence, for instance, of the discharge of solid materials by commercial concerns, which could sink in time to the bottom and become obstructions to navigation. This part of the act is also concerned with abandoned or derelict ships or barges which could become obstructions to navigation.
Part three is concerned primarily with ferry cables and swinging bridges. The amendments to the Navigable Waters Protection Act proposed in Bill S-19 are designed to bring the act up to date and make it easier to administer, and particularly to ensure that navigable waters remain navigable for the larger ships which are being constructed today as well as ships of shallower draft than
January 22, 1969

those which were in existence at the time the legislation was first enacted.
Perhaps I should emphasize that this is really one of the most important points of these amendments. Ships today are larger; therefore they take more water. They also move faster and therefore sometimes need a wider channel in which to travel. The regulations that were made for smaller ships do not apply or are not satisfactory for today's larger ships.
Some of the amendments which we will discuss are of a technical nature and we will have the opportunity to examine them in detail when the bill is considered by the standing committee. In presenting this legislation I should like to outline the highlights of the bill by referring to the more important amendments which I propose.
Clause 2 includes in the definition of a "work" the dumping of fill and any excavation of materials from the bed of a navigable water. In various areas of the country fill has been dumped into navigable waters without approval first having been obtained under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. The act as presently worded did not cover activities of this kind. Clause 3 establishes the time limit following ministerial approval for construction of any work. This will prevent any unnecessary delay in the construction of a work for which approval has been given. Section 4 of the present act makes reference to the over-all work not exceeding $5,000. The amendment which is proposed eliminates any reference to the dollar value of a work.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The reason is that since the act is concerned with the protection of navigable waters, interference with navigation should be the only test applied to the construction of any work and its monetary value should have no bearing on the matter. The amendment proposed will require that all works being built in navigable waters, regardless of their cost, will require approval or exemption. I might elaborate briefly and say that I understand one of the problems with the $5,000 figure was that there was often as much argument about whether the work was worth $4,000 or $6,000 as there was about whether it was an obstruction to navigation. Really, therefore the amendment is going to get at the main purpose of the act.
Section 5 of the act deals with the removal of unauthorized works and with approval of 29180-295
Navigable Waters Protection Act works already constructed. At the present time, if any work is built contrary to the provisions of the act the minister's alternatives are these: (1) to remove the work at the expense of the owner; (2) to give approval to it after a period of five years; (3) to allow it to continue to exist without approval. The proposed amendments to the act, in addition to the power of removal now contained in the act, would give the minister authority to order the owner to alter a work. That is the key change; the work now can be altered and does not have to be removed in total. If the owner fails to remove or alter the work, the minister would have authority to remove or alter it at the cost of the owner and to render the owner liable to a penalty recoverable upon summary conviction.
Clause 7 of the bill extends the authority of the Governor in Council to make regulations under section 10 of the act and provides for a scale of fees for temporary approval whenever immediate inspection trips are required. Provision is made also for a scale of fees for late application for approval; that is, of course, applications which have been made after construction has commenced or has been completed.
I would particularly like to point out that clause 10 of the bill amends sections 18 and
19	of the act. The purpose of the amendment to section 18 is to extend the application of the section to all persons. At the present time it applies primarily to saw mills. The purpose of the amendment to section 19 is to ensure that this section applies to tidal as well as non-tidal navigable waters, and to increase to
20	fathoms the depth of water in which no substance liable to sink may be thrown. The limit of the depth has been increased from 12 to 20 fathoms in order to protect the new, deep draught, bulk carriers now coming into use.
In clause 14 of the bill the penalties under sections 26, 27 and 28 of the act are being revised upward to provide a more realistic figure and to provide the act with more force.
As hon. members know, this bill has been considered and passed in the other place. I should point out also that it was referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications of the other place.
I would like to conclude the introduction of this legislation by emphasizing that Bill S-19, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act, is primarily a bill to tidy up the existing legislation in this field. It does not include major proposals for change of either policy or

Navigable Waters Protection Act principle, but it is useful and progressive legislation and I recommend the bill for the consideration of the house.

Mr. Speaker, before I deal briefly with some of the proposals contained in this bill I should like to bring to the attention of the house a suggestion just made to me by my friend the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). He suggested that when the government is considering future proposals or changes to acts and regulations of this type, it might well pay heed to the fact that today rivers and lakes are used by aircraft. I know this question is dealt with in other legislative proposals and regulations but it is one that might well be considered further. I mention it because we have just finished dealing with a bill amending the Aeronautics Act. My experience in flying in the north over the last 35 years or so leads me to believe there are circumstances and places with regard to which navigation was thought of strictly in terms of vessels rather than aircraft when this act was passed.
There are two aspects of this bill that I want to very briefly bring to the attention of the house. The first is that the bill is carrying a step further the practice of this government of putting into statutes and bills more and more often the right of the government to act by order in council, to act by ministerial decree. This matter was referred to in the discussion on the bill with which we just dealt and it has been mentioned in connection with other bills. If one wanted to compile a litany of the proposals in which this very iniquitous principle can be observed, he would have only to examine the list of legislative proposals which have been presented to this house over the few months since the 28th parliament met in September.
I shall not detail the bills now because there will be another opportunity, perhaps more suitable and one when I shall be more in order to deal with the question. If one looks at the list of bills we have passed he finds that slowly, insidiously and with great care and planning there has been taking place the pleasant seduction of the twenty eighth parliament by the government seeking and being given rights which in many instances should belong to parliament. To some extent this is observed in the bill we are now considering. It may be nice to have a situation wherein the head of the government is showing to our fascinated eyes spectacular conduct, but while this is taking place and we are (Mr. Richardson.]
looking at what is happening there, parliament is being filched of its rights.
It will be my purpose before this parliament is over to detail in very considerable measure all the proposals in question from the beginning of the parliament to the end and the rights which have been taken away from us. I shall indicate where this parliament has given to the government, without any recourse, discretionary control over so many aspects of our life and society, but that must wait.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with this bill in the light of a particular problem that has presented itself in my area and indeed in the whole of northwestern Canada. I wonder just how effective the Navigable Waters Protection Act is, or can be, under certain conditions which prevail. Some years ago the government of British Columbia, the government of Canada and that of the United States were negotiating with regard to the use of rivers for the production and generation of power in British Columbia. They included the Peace River and the Columbia River. Proceedings had come to a standstill and the governments changed. At that time, the then secretary of state for external affairs, now the leader of the government in the Senate, in his desperate anxiety to see that this project went forward entered into what I believe to be a very reprehensible arrangement with the government of the province of British Columbia to permit an obstruction to be placed across the Peace River in breach of this act.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
This has been a navigable river, to my knowledge and from reading history, since Alexander Mackenzie, the first white man to come down the Peace River, cross the Rocky Mountains and go overland to the Pacific. He came down the Peace River in 1791. An arrangement was made under which the province of British Columbia was allowed to place a dam across the Peace River in the vicinity of Hudson Hope. At that time I asked the minister of justice and the minister of public works, who then had responsibility for the administration of this act, whether or not what was being planned by the province of B.C. did in fact constitute the sort of work at which the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act was directed. The answer was yes, it did. On a number of occasions I asked the then minister of public works, the hon. Mr. Deschatelets, now a very distinguished
January 22, 1969	COMMONS
member of the other place and who approached this in a very sincere way, whether any attempt was to be made to compel the province of B.C. to secure the consent which was required under this act.
I will relate this situation to the amendments which are now proposed as I develop my case. Despite the fact that the answers were always in the affirmative and that there was never at any time any suggestion that the damming of the Peace River and the related works for the purpose of generating power were not works to which this act applied, it was always admitted that no application was made and none was ever requested. I think this is a fantastic thing. I talk about this because I can recall the very last case which I had to deal with as a member of the bar. I was to appear for a farmer who had a small cattle ranch in the vicinity of Lesser Slave Lake. A very tiny creek passed through his pasture, so he fenced it in order to keep in his cattle. He got into an argument with the local federal department of public works officials who told him that while this was a small stream it was a navigable stream in the sense that there was a fisherman's boat a few hundred yards up stream. Three or four times a year this fisherman brought his boat downstream into Lesser Slave Lake. This farmer was a man of some principle, and he believed in fighting for what he thought was right. He opposed the position taken by the federal people. The matter went to the Exchequer Court of Canada and it was held, as of course it must be held under the act, that this was a navigable water. So, the farmer was compelled to take down his fence and pay the cost.
Three or four years later the province of British Columbia, because of the fact the then Secretary of State for External Affairs was ambitious to bring to what he hoped would be a successful conclusion these negotiations dealing with the erection of a power dam at Peace River, was allowed to completely disregard the provisions of this act. It was a flagrant violation.
I find that the new bill provides in one of its clauses that where a work has been placed without authority, the federal government may seek to have it destroyed or pulled down. I am not so bold as to suggest that this government would be able to do this, even if it wanted to tackle Mr. Bennet. There seems to be something about the provinces in either extremity of this country. Perhaps it is due to the fact that they sit on the beaches, look 29180-2951

Navigable Waters Protection Act across the waves coming in and in this way acquire the characteristics of King Canute. They feel they can compel anything to happen, even the waves to go back. But for anyone to tackle either Mr. Smallwood or Mr. Bennet is quite an undertaking, and I do not think even a government dedicated to the just society would do this.
There is a change which is proposed here in clause 5 which reads:
Where any work to which this Part applies is built or placed without having been approved by the Minister or is built or placed upon a site not approved by the Minister or is not built or placed in accordance with plans so approved, or having been so built or placed, is not maintained in accordance with such plans and the regulations, the Minister-
This means the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer). The Minister of Transport is of course also a very determined man and I do not know what happens when an irresistible force tries to move an immovable body. If this clause means anything, then it means the Minister of Transport would be within his legal rights in making this request of the B.C. government. But we all know this is not going to take place.
Since the dam was completed across this navigable river it has created one of the largest reservoirs in the country, and possibly in the north American continent, flowing back to the Rocky Mountain trench and up and down it for several miles. It will be a tremendously large body of water. In the last two or three years an attempt has been made to fill the reservoir. As a result, every summer the waters of the Peace River have been exceptionally low. It has been a ghastly sight, for anyone who has seen the beauty of these northern rivers, to drive along the course of the river and see what has happened. It is predicted the filling of this reservoir will have disastrous effects, not only on the hinterland between the Rocky Mountains but where the Peace River enters into the Slave River. It will have serious effects on the water level of Lake Athabasca and the whole Mackenzie River system. This has been confirmed by statements made by people living in the Yellowknife and Great Slave Lake area. It is obvious to anyone who travels along the river and has seen what has happened. It is all very well for the officials of the federal government or possibly of the B.C. government to say that once the reservoir has been filled this situation will not recur.

However, it is not possible to make that prediction with any accuracy because if, during the course of the calendar year there is not the rainfall and snowfall which is required to provide enough water in the dam, then the water which will be released will not be adequate to provide the navigable aspect of the river which is so essential.
I use the occasion of this amendment, as I think I am entitled to do to bring this very forcibly to the attention of the government because it does not simply affect one town and a few farmers; it affects thousands of people who use the river. We hear about the proposal to explore and establish potentially commercially feasible oil development fields in northern Canada and northern United States. It is very likely that the whole Mackenzie Biver system will be dedicated in part to both carrying traffic into that area and possibly taking commodities out. I think it is tremendously important for this reason.
So I hope that because of these amendments, combined with the original legislation, the government will look at this very carefully. I have been in correspondence with the government, but it is quite obvious that the government's view is that the province of B.C. occupies the area and so far it has shown no willingness to give effect to the great number of representations which have been made.
[DOT] (5:50 p.ra.)
I now suggest to the government in the face of this amendment and of the existing legislation that if this bill and the original act are to be considered as being of any value, this is a grave situation which must be dealt with both by the federal government and by the Province of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with a great deal of interest to what was said by the previous speaker in connection with the Peace River. I, too, wonder just how effective legislation under the Navigable Waters Protection Act has been in providing protection for the rivers and waterways which it is supposed to control.
Many of the amendments offered in this bill are good ones, but I certainly endorse the words of the previous speaker when he complained about the increasing use of orders in council by governments in both the federal and provincial fields. In this case, of course, we are referring to the federal field. I notice that in clause seven, of which we have been

given a brief explanation, there is one sentence which appears to be of significance; I hope it means what it says. I reads:
The governor in Council may make such orders and regulations as he deems expedient for navigation purposes respecting any work to which this part applies.
Recently I encountered a problem, as did the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), in connection with this aspect of the legislation. I placed a question on the order paper and it was finally answered by, of all people, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene). As far as I could make out it had nothing to do with his department; it had to do with navigation along the Columbia River. I should like to pose the following question to the minister because it relates very closely to this bill: just who establishes, for example, the schedule of times at which locks in the Arrow Dam may be used? This is a simple question which a number of organizations in my area have been asking over the last four months. We still have not received a satisfactory answer from the government. I am confident that responsibility lies within the Department of Transport under this legislation. We have been given the run-around from department to department and no one seems to know just who is making the regulations, how they were made, when they were made, and for what purpose they were made.
The other day, in connection with this set of regulations, I asked the following questions:
1.	Was the Columbia River at the site of the Arrow Dam open to year-round river traffic prior to the dam construction?
2.	Is the operation of the lock in the Arrow Dam on a year-round basis and, if not (a) what is the present schedule (b) when was it put into effect?
The answer given to each of these questions was, yes.
Mr. Speaker, this is not correct information. The answers given to this house and to the public of Canada are not correct. The locks on the Arrow Dam are not on a year round sechdule. The schedule is drawn up, apparently, by the British Columbia Hydro Authority, and these locks are open from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. on days other than holidays and weekends.
Need I point out that it is precisely at weekends and on holidays that the public wishes to use these locks to take boats into the huge reservoir basin above the dam. Yet
January 22, 19S9

this is when access is being denied them. It is amazing to come here to Ottawa and find the department knows practically nothing about the setting up of this schedule, which, it appears, was drawn up by the Hydro crown corporation back in British Columbia. It makes one wonder what kind of hold the premier of British Columbia has on this government.
British Columbia Hydro pays the shot for the operation of the locks. I want to say here that the entire area below the Arrow Dam is concerned about the schedule and about the use of these locks. We shall not be satisfied with a four or five day week, and only limited opportunity to use these locks to reach the lake, some hundred miles in length, which lies above the dam. If the terms of the legislation before us will not permit anything effective to be done about this situation, I think the minister should take another close look as them.
I notice that a number of sections in the act have been changed. The Governor in Council is again given permission to exempt certain navigable waters from the terms of the legislation. It is in this connection, I presume, that the hon. member for Peace River is encountering trouble.
